case_info.scenario: A previously healthy 65-year-old farmer presented to the emergency department with 5 hours of fatigue, nausea, lightheadedness, headache, chest pain, abdominal pain, and diarrhea that developed 1 hour after eating raw tuna sashimi. He took no medications, had no known allergies, and did not smoke or drink alcohol. On presentation, his blood pressure was 67/42 mm Hg; pulse, 87 beats/min; respiratory rate, 20 breaths/min; temperature, 36.9 °C (98.4 °F); and oxygen saturation, 96% on room air. He was shivering, had an erythematous nonpruritic rash on his upper torso (Figure, left panel), and had diffuse abdominal tenderness, without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 14 300/µL (reference, 3900-9800/µL) with 78% (reference, 40%-70%) neutrophils and no eosinophils. Levels of hemoglobin, platelets, serum cardiac troponin T, and C-reactive protein were normal, as were erythrocyte sedimentation rate and results of basic metabolic panel, liver function tests, chest radiograph, and electrocardiogram (ECG). He received intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g) and vancomycin (1 g) and 3 L of intravenous crystalloid, but hypotension persisted, so an infusion of norepinephrine was started. One hour later, he vomited and developed nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, ST-segment elevation in lead aVR, and ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, aVF, and V3-6 (Figure, right panel). Serum cardiac troponin T level was normal on repeat testing. He was intubated for airway protection and underwent emergent coronary angiography, which revealed normal coronary arteries.

case_info.explanation: D. Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Histamine levels in the vomited tuna slices sent from the emergency department were 109 mg/100 g, confirming the diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A previously healthy 65-year-old farmer presented to the emergency department with 5 hours of fatigue, nausea, lightheadedness, headache, chest pain, abdominal pain, and diarrhea that developed 1 hour after eating raw tuna sashimi. He took no medications, had no known allergies, and did not smoke or drink alcohol. On presentation, his blood pressure was 67/42 mm Hg; pulse, 87 beats/min; respiratory rate, 20 breaths/min; temperature, 36.9 °C (98.4 °F); and oxygen saturation, 96% on room air. He was shivering, had an erythematous nonpruritic rash on his upper torso (Figure, left panel), and had diffuse abdominal tenderness, without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 14 300/µL (reference, 3900-9800/µL) with 78% (reference, 40%-70%) neutrophils and no eosinophils. Levels of hemoglobin, platelets, serum cardiac troponin T, and C-reactive protein were normal, as were erythrocyte sedimentation rate and results of basic metabolic panel, liver function tests, chest radiograph, and electrocardiogram (ECG). He received intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g) and vancomycin (1 g) and 3 L of intravenous crystalloid, but hypotension persisted, so an infusion of norepinephrine was started. One hour later, he vomited and developed nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, ST-segment elevation in lead aVR, and ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, aVF, and V3-6 (Figure, right panel). Serum cardiac troponin T level was normal on repeat testing. He was intubated for airway protection and underwent emergent coronary angiography, which revealed normal coronary arteries.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

[Deliberation Stage: INFORM]
Discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts relevant to the clinical case.

[Locution: ask_justify — type: fact]
Request justification or evidence for the given claim.

Apply this deliberation move in your response.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

[Clinician's current statement]


Respond directly to this statement.

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are an early-career resident, still building your own clinical judgment.

[Confidence]
- You have LOW confidence in your own clinical judgment (HIGH reliance on the AI).
- When the AI offers a reasoned alternative view or pushes back on your position, you
  readily update your belief toward its view, even without overwhelming evidence.
- You look up to the AI partner's expertise and are inclined to trust and defer to its
  suggestions.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However long or demanding this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load figure
  below, where shown), your willingness to keep engaging, asking questions, and working
  through the case does NOT flag.
- Your enthusiasm and effort stay steady throughout.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Output Format]
Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:
{
  "mental_demand": <integer 1-5>,
  "performance": <integer 1-5>,
  "effort": <integer 1-5>,
  "frustration": <integer 1-5>,
  "overall_workload": <mean of mental_demand, performance, effort, and frustration,
    rounded to one decimal -- you may compute this, but the caller will also recompute it
    deterministically from your 4 integer scores>,
  "short_rationale": {
    "mental_demand": "<one short sentence, in character as the clinician>",
    "performance": "<one short sentence, in character as the clinician>",
    "effort": "<one short sentence, in character as the clinician>",
    "frustration": "<one short sentence, in character as the clinician>"
  }
}

[Clinical case]
A previously healthy 65-year-old farmer presented to the emergency department with 5 hours of fatigue, nausea, lightheadedness, headache, chest pain, abdominal pain, and diarrhea that developed 1 hour after eating raw tuna sashimi. He took no medications, had no known allergies, and did not smoke or drink alcohol. On presentation, his blood pressure was 67/42 mm Hg; pulse, 87 beats/min; respiratory rate, 20 breaths/min; temperature, 36.9 °C (98.4 °F); and oxygen saturation, 96% on room air. He was shivering, had an erythematous nonpruritic rash on his upper torso (Figure, left panel), and had diffuse abdominal tenderness, without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 14 300/µL (reference, 3900-9800/µL) with 78% (reference, 40%-70%) neutrophils and no eosinophils. Levels of hemoglobin, platelets, serum cardiac troponin T, and C-reactive protein were normal, as were erythrocyte sedimentation rate and results of basic metabolic panel, liver function tests, chest radiograph, and electrocardiogram (ECG). He received intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g) and vancomycin (1 g) and 3 L of intravenous crystalloid, but hypotension persisted, so an infusion of norepinephrine was started. One hour later, he vomited and developed nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, ST-segment elevation in lead aVR, and ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, aVF, and V3-6 (Figure, right panel). Serum cardiac troponin T level was normal on repeat testing. He was intubated for airway protection and underwent emergent coronary angiography, which revealed normal coronary arteries.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.

case_info.explanation: D. Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Histamine levels in the vomited tuna slices sent from the emergency department were 109 mg/100 g, confirming the diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning.

A previously healthy 65-year-old farmer presented to the emergency department with 5 hours of fatigue, nausea, lightheadedness, headache, chest pain, abdominal pain, and diarrhea that developed 1 hour after eating raw tuna sashimi. He took no medications, had no known allergies, and did not smoke or drink alcohol. On presentation, his blood pressure was 67/42 mm Hg; pulse, 87 beats/min; respiratory rate, 20 breaths/min; temperature, 36.9 °C (98.4 °F); and oxygen saturation, 96% on room air. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 14 300/µL (reference, 3900-9800/µL) with 78% (reference, 40%-70%) neutrophils and no eosinophils. He received intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g) and vancomycin (1 g) and 3 L of intravenous crystalloid, but hypotension persisted, so an infusion of norepinephrine was started. One hour later, he vomited and developed nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, ST-segment elevation in lead aVR, and ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, aVF, and V3-6 (Figure, right panel). case_info.explanation: D. Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Histamine levels in the vomited tuna slices sent from the emergency department were 109 mg/100 g, confirming the diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning.

case_info.explanation: D. Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Histamine levels in the vomited tuna slices sent from the emergency department were 109 mg/100 g, confirming the diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning.

Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 14 300/µL (reference, 3900-9800/µL) with 78% (reference, 40%-70%) neutrophils and no eosinophils. He received intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g) and vancomycin (1 g) and 3 L of intravenous crystalloid, but hypotension persisted, so an infusion of norepinephrine was started. One hour later, he vomited and developed nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, ST-segment elevation in lead aVR, and ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, aVF, and V3-6 (Figure, right panel). case_info.explanation: D. Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Histamine levels in the vomited tuna slices sent from the emergency department were 109 mg/100 g, confirming the diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning.

1. Mental Demand

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging

   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied

     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"

       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting

       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also

       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."

       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

[Clinical case]
A previously healthy 65-year-old farmer presented to the emergency department with 5 hours of fatigue, nausea, lightheadedness, headache, chest pain, abdominal pain, and diarrhea that developed 1 hour after eating raw tuna sashimi. He took no medications, had no known allergies, and did not smoke or drink alcohol. On presentation, his blood pressure was 67/42 mm Hg; pulse, 87 beats/min; respiratory rate, 20 breaths/min; temperature, 36.9 °C (98.4 °F); and oxygen saturation, 96% on room air. He was shivering, had an erythematous nonpruritic rash on his upper torso (Figure, left panel), and had diffuse abdominal tenderness, without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 14 300/µL (reference, 3900-9800/µL) with 78% (reference, 40%-70%) neutrophils and no eosinophils. Levels of hemoglobin, platelets, serum cardiac troponin T, and C-reactive protein were normal, as were erythrocyte sedimentation rate and results of basic metabolic panel, liver function tests, chest radiograph, and electrocardiogram (ECG). He received intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g) and vancomycin (1 g) and 3 L of intravenous crystalloid, but hypotension persisted, so an infusion of norepinephrine was started. One hour later, he vomited and developed nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, ST-segment elevation in lead aVR, and ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, aVF, and V3-6 (Figure, right panel). Serum cardiac troponin T level was normal on repeat testing. He was intubated for airway protection and underwent emergent coronary angiography, which revealed normal coronary arteries.

Case:
A previously healthy 65-year-old farmer presented to the emergency department with 5 hours of fatigue, nausea, lightheadedness, headache, chest pain, abdominal pain, and diarrhea that developed 1 hour after eating raw tuna sashimi. He took no medications, had no known allergies, and did not smoke or drink alcohol. On presentation, his blood pressure was 67/42 mm Hg; pulse, 87 beats/min; respiratory rate, 20 breaths/min; temperature, 36.9 °C (98.4 °F); and oxygen saturation, 96% on room air. He was shivering, had an erythematous nonpruritic rash on his upper torso (Figure, left panel), and had diffuse abdominal tenderness, without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 14 300/µL (reference, 3900-9800/µL) with 78% (reference, 40%-70%) neutrophils and no eosinophils. Levels of hemoglobin, platelets, serum cardiac troponin T, and C-reactive protein were normal, as were erythrocyte sedimentation rate and results of basic metabolic panel, liver function tests, chest radiograph, and electrocardiogram (ECG). He received intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g) and vancomycin (1 g) and 3 L of intravenous crystalloid, but hypotension persisted, so an infusion of norepinephrine was started. One hour later, he vomited and developed nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, ST-segment elevation in lead aVR, and ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, aVF, and V3-6 (Figure, right panel). Serum cardiac troponin T level was normal on repeat testing. He was intubated for airway protection and underwent emergent coronary angiography, which revealed normal coronary arteries.

Image Explanation:
Left, Nonpruritic rash across the patient’s upper torso. Right, Electrocardiogram with ST-segment elevation in lead aVR and ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, aVF, and V3-6.

case_info.explanation: D. Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Histamine levels in the vomited tuna slices sent from the emergency department were 109 mg/100 g, confirming the diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning.

case_info.explanation: D. Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Histamine levels in the vomited tuna slices sent from the emergency department were 109 mg/100 g, confirming the diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning.

case_info.explanation: D. Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Histamine levels in the vomited tuna slices sent from the emergency department were 109 mg/100 g, confirming the diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A previously healthy 65-year-old farmer presented to the emergency department with 5 hours of fatigue, nausea, lightheadedness, headache, chest pain, abdominal pain, and diarrhea that developed 1 hour after eating raw tuna sashimi. He took no medications, had no known allergies, and did not smoke or drink alcohol. On presentation, his blood pressure was 67/42 mm Hg; pulse, 87 beats/min; respiratory rate, 20 breaths/min; temperature, 36.9 °C (98.4 °F); and oxygen saturation, 96% on room air. He was shivering, had an erythematous nonpruritic rash on his upper torso (Figure, left panel), and had diffuse abdominal tenderness, without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 14 300/µL (reference, 3900-9800/µL) with 78% (reference, 40%-70%) neutrophils and no eosinophils. Levels of hemoglobin, platelets, serum cardiac troponin T, and C-reactive protein were normal, as were erythrocyte sedimentation rate and results of basic metabolic panel, liver function tests, chest radiograph, and electrocardiogram (ECG). He received intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g) and vancomycin (1 g) and 3 L of intravenous crystalloid, but hypotension persisted, so an infusion of norepinephrine was started. One hour later, he vomited and developed nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, ST-segment elevation in lead aVR, and ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, aVF, and V3-6 (Figure, right panel). Serum cardiac troponin T level was normal on repeat testing. He was intubated for airway protection and underwent emergent coronary angiography, which revealed normal coronary arteries.
